title: Salutation to the Merciful
hookLine: namastvam kripaale: salutation to the Merciful One (Jaap, bhujang prayat)

lines: A FINE, A TICKET, A LATE ASSIGNMENT.
DON'T WORRY ABOUT IT THIS TIME.
A DOOR WHERE YOU EXPECTED A WALL.
cards: A parking ticket, a library fine, a late assignment. You walk up ready to argue, already tired, and the person behind the counter looks at you, looks at the clock, and says: don't worry about it this time. No speech.

Just a small door opening where you expected a wall. Moments like that tend to stay; mercy has a way of doing that. And in Jaap Sahib, right after the bow to the One beyond time, comes a bow to exactly this.

teach.b: The line is namastvam kripaale: a bow to you, the Merciful. Kripaal comes from kirpa, or kripa: grace, kindness, mercy, favor you didn't earn. Kripaal is the One who is full of it.
Now notice the order. The first line bowed to akaal, the One the clock can't touch. That could sound cold, a God too big and too far away to care about a parking ticket.
So the very next line answers it.
Timeless, yes. And merciful. In Sikh teaching those two ideas belong together.

Guru Nanak's hymns speak of nadar, the glance of grace, the kind look that lifts a person when their own effort has run out. Japji, which you walked through last year, says liberation comes through that grace.
And kirpa is everywhere in Punjabi life, not just in prayer books.

teach.h: WAHEGURU DI KIRPA NAAL: BY GRACE.
teach.b: Ask a Sikh grandmother how the family is doing, and you may well hear: Waheguru di kirpa naal, theek haan. By Waheguru's grace, we're fine.
A new job, a healthy baby, a safe journey, all described as kirpa, a way of saying: this wasn't only my doing. And it has a practical edge.
Some Sikhs hear a question tucked inside the bow: if the One I salute every morning is merciful, where could I open a small door instead of a wall today? Jaap doesn't say that in so many words.
It just puts mercy second in the glide, right after eternity.

how: Sikhs speak of good things in daily life as kirpa, grace, often saying Waheguru di kirpa naal, by Waheguru's grace, and recite namastvam kripaale each morning in Jaap Sahib.

o: a small sword every Khalsa Sikh wears
merciful, the One full of grace
a hymn sung only at weddings

games.q: salutation to the Merciful — tap the pairs.

s: Jaap salutes the Merciful before the Timeless
akaal comes first, then kripaal, right after it.
kirpa is a word used in everyday Punjabi, not just in prayer
a new job or a safe journey is often described as kirpa, grace.
Guru Nanak's hymns speak of nadar, the glance of grace
the kind look that lifts a person when their own effort has run out.

games.q: Jaap has just bowed to the Timeless, the One the clock can't touch. a listener worries: is this God too far away to care? what does the next line say?
games.why: namastvam kripaale: Jaap pairs them, timeless and merciful, one line after the other.

practice: Think of someone who owes you something, an apology, an answer, a borrowed thing, or who's been a little careless with you lately, and picture their face as you breathe.
Decide, quietly, to let one small thing go, the way the person at the counter did: not everything, just one. If you pray, you can say namastvam kripaale under your breath, then rest.

wordCard.voice: Kripaal. Merciful, full of kirpa, grace — namastvam kripaale, the second bow of Jaap's glide, right after the bow to the Timeless.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kripaal, merciful, the One full of kirpa, grace.

carryVoice: Your line: salute mercy. Timeless, and merciful, side by side in the glide. Day three hundred thirty-eight.
